title: Polity Complete 1: Framework, FR, DPSP, FD

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Regulating Act of 1773 provided for the establishment of a Supreme Court at Calcutta.
2. The Pitt's India Act of 1784 created a Board of Control to supervise the political affairs of the East India Company.
3. The Charter Act of 1813 ended the Company's trade monopoly in India as well as in tea and the China trade.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: The 1773 Act set up a Supreme Court at Calcutta, and the 1784 Act created the Board of Control (political) while leaving commercial matters with the Directors, a dual system. The 1813 Act ended the monopoly in Indian trade but kept the Company's monopoly in tea and the China trade, which went only in 1833.
questions.h: 1773 Court, 1784 Board, 1813 trade (not tea), 1833 all commerce ends

questions.q:
Statement-I: The Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909 are said to have legalised communalism in Indian politics.
Statement-II: The Government of India Act of 1919 extended separate electorates to Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
questions.e: The 1909 Act introduced separate electorates for Muslims, which is why Lord Minto is called the father of communal electorate. The 1919 Act is a later development that widened the principle to other communities; it does not explain why the 1909 Act is said to have legalised communalism.

questions.q:
With reference to the Government of India Act of 1935, consider the following statements:
1. It abolished dyarchy in the provinces and introduced it at the Centre.
2. It provided for the establishment of a Federal Court.
3. The All-India Federation envisaged by it came into existence in 1937.
4. It abolished the Council of India that had advised the Secretary of State for India.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Provincial autonomy replaced provincial dyarchy, dyarchy was introduced at the Centre, a Federal Court was set up and the Council of India was abolished. The proposed All-India Federation never came into being because the princely states did not agree to join; only the provincial part of the Act was implemented in 1937.

questions.q:
With reference to the making of the Indian Constitution, consider the following statements:
1. The Objective Resolution moved by Jawaharlal Nehru was adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 22 January 1947.
2. The Drafting Committee was set up on 29 August 1947 with B. R. Ambedkar as its Chairman.
3. The entire Constitution came into force on the day it was adopted, 26 November 1949.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Nehru moved the Objective Resolution on 13 December 1946 and it was adopted on 22 January 1947; the Drafting Committee was set up on 29 August 1947. On 26 November 1949 only provisions on citizenship, elections, the provisional Parliament, temporary and transitional provisions and a few others came into force; the rest came into force on 26 January 1950.

questions.q: Under which of the following Acts did the 'Governor-General of Bengal' become the 'Governor-General of India', with Lord William Bentinck as the first holder of the new office?
questions.e: The Charter Act of 1833 centralised the administration by making the Governor-General of Bengal the Governor-General of India, vested with all civil and military powers. It also ended the Company's commercial functions. The 1858 Act later created the office of Viceroy.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the Preamble:
1. In the Berubari Union case (1960), the Supreme Court held that the Preamble is not a part of the Constitution.
2. In the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973), the Supreme Court held that the Preamble is a part of the Constitution.
3. The Preamble is a source of power for the legislature and also a prohibition upon its powers.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Berubari said the Preamble is a key to the minds of the makers but not a part of the Constitution; Kesavananda overruled this and held it is a part and can be amended without altering the basic structure. In Berubari the Court also said the Preamble is neither a source of power nor a limitation or prohibition on the legislature, so statement 3 is wrong.
questions.h: Berubari: key but not part; Kesavananda: part

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Preamble of the Indian Constitution:
1. It has been amended only once so far.
2. The 42nd Amendment Act added the words 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'Integrity'.
3. It mentions the date of adoption of the Constitution as 26 November 1949.
4. The word 'Republic' was added to it by the 42nd Amendment Act.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: The Preamble was amended once, in 1976, which inserted 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'Integrity' (unity of the Nation became unity and integrity of the Nation). 'Republic' was in the original text, so statement 4 is wrong. The adoption date 26 November 1949 appears in the last line.

questions.q: According to Laxmikanth, the ideal of 'Justice - social, economic and political' in the Preamble has been taken from the
questions.e: The ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity come from the French Revolution, while the ideal of justice (social, economic and political) is traced to the Russian Revolution of 1917.
questions.h: Justice from Russia; LEF from France

questions.q:
Statement-I: India is described in the Preamble as a 'Republic'.
Statement-II: The head of the Indian State is elected for a fixed term and the office is not hereditary.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
questions.e: A republic is a polity in which the head of State is elected, directly or indirectly, for a fixed term rather than holding a hereditary office. The President of India is indirectly elected for five years, which is exactly why India is called a republic.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 3 of the Constitution:
1. A Bill under Article 3 can be introduced in Parliament only on the recommendation of the President.
2. The views of the concerned State Legislature on such a Bill are binding on Parliament.
3. A law made under Article 3 is not deemed to be an amendment of the Constitution under Article 368.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: The Bill needs the President's recommendation and must be referred to the State Legislature for its views, but the President or Parliament is not bound by them. Article 4 says such laws are not amendments under Article 368, so they need only a simple majority.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Supreme Court in the Berubari Union case held that Parliament can cede Indian territory to a foreign country by a law under Article 3.
2. The 100th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2015 gave effect to the land boundary agreement with Bangladesh.
3. In clauses (a) to (e) of Article 3, the expression 'State' includes a Union Territory.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: In Berubari the Court held that Article 3 covers internal readjustment of States, not cession of territory to a foreign country, which needs an amendment under Article 368 (the 9th Amendment followed). The 100th Amendment gave effect to the India-Bangladesh land boundary agreement, and the Explanation to Article 3 says 'State' includes a Union Territory in clauses (a) to (e).

questions.q:
Arrange the following in the chronological order of their attaining statehood:
1. Haryana
2. Nagaland
3. Himachal Pradesh
4. Sikkim
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.e: Nagaland became a State in 1963, Haryana was carved out of Punjab in 1966, Himachal Pradesh got full statehood in 1971 and Sikkim became a State in 1975 through the 36th Amendment (after being an associate State under the 35th Amendment in 1974).

questions.q:
With reference to the reorganisation of States in India, consider the following statements:
1. The States Reorganisation Commission of 1953 was headed by Fazl Ali.
2. The Commission accepted language as the sole basis for the reorganisation of States.
3. The States Reorganisation Act, 1956 created 14 States and 6 Union Territories.
4. The Dhar Commission of 1948 recommended reorganisation of States purely on linguistic lines.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: The Fazl Ali Commission (with K. M. Panikkar and H. N. Kunzru) accepted language as an important factor but rejected the 'one language, one State' principle, and the 1956 Act created 14 States and 6 Union Territories. The Dhar Commission had actually favoured administrative convenience over linguistic reorganisation.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding citizenship in India:
1. Citizenship is a subject on which only Parliament can legislate.
2. Articles 5 to 9 of the Constitution deal with citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution.
3. The Constitution lays down detailed rules on acquisition and termination of citizenship after its commencement.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Citizenship, naturalisation and aliens are in the Union List, and Article 11 empowers Parliament to regulate the matter, which it did through the Citizenship Act, 1955. The Constitution itself covers only citizenship at its commencement; later acquisition and loss are left to Parliament.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019:
1. It reduced the aggregate residence requirement for naturalisation of specified migrants from 11 years to 5 years.
2. It applies to specified migrants who entered India on or before 31 December 2014.
3. It does not apply to tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram and Tripura included in the Sixth Schedule.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: The Act covers Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis and Christians from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan who entered by 31 December 2014, and reduced their residence requirement from 11 to 5 years. Sixth Schedule tribal areas and areas under the Inner Line Permit are exempted.

questions.q: Which one of the following is NOT a mode of loss of citizenship under the Citizenship Act, 1955?
questions.e: The Act provides for loss of citizenship by renunciation (voluntary), termination (on voluntarily acquiring foreign citizenship) and deprivation (compulsory, by the Central Government). Expulsion is not a statutory mode of loss.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Constitutional provisions on citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution:
1. Persons who migrated from Pakistan after 19 July 1948 became citizens automatically under Article 6.
2. Certain persons who migrated to Pakistan after 1 March 1947 but later returned to India for resettlement under a permit could become citizens under Article 7.
3. Persons of Indian origin residing outside India could become citizens under Article 8 by registration with the diplomatic or consular representative.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Migrants from Pakistan who came before 19 July 1948 were deemed citizens; those who came on or after that date had to register after six months' residence, so statement 1 is wrong. Article 7 covers returnees under a resettlement permit and Article 8 covers persons of Indian origin abroad, through registration.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 13 of the Constitution:
1. The term 'law' in Article 13 includes ordinances, bye-laws, rules, regulations, notifications and customs having the force of law.
2. A law inconsistent with a Fundamental Right is void only to the extent of the inconsistency.
3. In the Kesavananda Bharati case, the Supreme Court held that a constitutional amendment is a 'law' within the meaning of Article 13.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Article 13(3) defines 'law' widely and Article 13 makes inconsistent laws void to the extent of the conflict. Golaknath (1967) had treated an amendment as 'law', but Kesavananda (1973) held that an amendment under Article 368 is not 'law' under Article 13, though it cannot alter the basic structure.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 14:
1. A classification under Article 14 must rest on an intelligible differentia.
2. The differentia must have a rational nexus with the object sought to be achieved by the law.
3. Article 14 permits class legislation.
4. Article 14 is available to non-citizens also.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Article 14 forbids class legislation but permits reasonable classification, which must satisfy the twin tests of intelligible differentia and rational nexus. 'Any person' is used in Article 14, so foreigners are covered too. Statement 3 confuses the two ideas.

questions.q:
Consider the following pairs:
Provision : Inserted by
1. Article 15(4) : First Amendment Act, 1951
2. Article 15(5) : 86th Amendment Act, 2002
3. Article 16(4A) : 77th Amendment Act, 1995
4. Article 15(6) : 103rd Amendment Act, 2019
How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
questions.e: Article 15(4) came after the Champakam Dorairajan case, 16(4A) (promotions for SC/ST) came through the 77th Amendment and 15(6) (economically weaker sections) through the 103rd. Article 15(5), on admission to educational institutions including private unaided ones, was inserted by the 93rd Amendment (2005); the 86th gave Article 21A.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding reservation in public employment:
1. In the Indra Sawhney case, the Supreme Court held that the 50 percent ceiling on reservation is absolute and cannot be exceeded in any circumstance.
2. The Court held that the 'creamy layer' among the Other Backward Classes must be excluded from reservation benefits.
3. The Supreme Court in Janhit Abhiyan (2022) upheld the 103rd Amendment providing 10 percent reservation for economically weaker sections by a 3:2 majority.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Indra Sawhney (1992) set the 50 percent limit as a general rule but allowed relaxation in extraordinary situations, so 'absolute' is wrong. It also required exclusion of the creamy layer, and in November 2022 a five-judge bench upheld the EWS quota by a 3:2 verdict.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 18:
1. It prohibits the State from conferring any title except a military or academic distinction.
2. No citizen of India can accept any title from a foreign State.
3. A non-citizen holding an office of profit under the State may accept a title from a foreign State without the consent of the President.
4. In the Balaji Raghavan case, the Supreme Court held that national awards such as the Bharat Ratna are titles prohibited by Article 18.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Article 18(1) and (2) bar the State from conferring titles (other than military or academic) and bar citizens from accepting foreign titles. A non-citizen holding an office of profit needs the President's consent (Article 18(3)), and Balaji Raghavan (1996) held that Bharat Ratna and Padma awards are not titles.

questions.q: Which one of the following is NOT expressly mentioned as a freedom in Article 19(1) of the Constitution?
o: Freedom to form associations or unions or co-operative societies
Freedom to assemble peacefully and without arms
Freedom to practise any profession or to carry on any occupation, trade or business
questions.e: Freedom of the press is not expressly listed; the Supreme Court read it into the freedom of speech and expression in Article 19(1)(a). The 97th Amendment added co-operative societies to Article 19(1)(c). The right to property was removed from Article 19 by the 44th Amendment.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 20:
1. The protection against ex post facto laws applies only to criminal laws and not to civil or tax laws.
2. The protection against double jeopardy does not apply to departmental or administrative proceedings.
3. The right against self-incrimination prohibits compelling an accused to give specimen handwriting or thumb impressions.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Ex post facto protection covers only convictions and penalties under criminal law, and double jeopardy applies only to prosecution and punishment before a court or judicial tribunal. In State of Bombay v. Kathi Kalu Oghad the Court held that giving specimen handwriting or thumb impressions is not testimonial compulsion, so statement 3 is wrong.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 21 and related provisions:
1. In Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, the Supreme Court held that 'procedure established by law' means any procedure laid down by the legislature, however arbitrary.
2. Article 21A, inserted by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002, provides free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14 years.
3. In the Puttaswamy case (2017), a nine-judge bench held that the right to privacy is an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Maneka Gandhi (1978) widened Article 21 by holding that the procedure must be fair, just and reasonable, which brought in a due-process flavour; it did not accept arbitrary procedure. Article 21A and the nine-judge Puttaswamy verdict are correctly stated.
questions.h: Maneka = fair procedure, not any procedure

questions.q:
Statement-I: The safeguards in Article 22(1) and 22(2), such as production before a magistrate within 24 hours and the right to consult a lawyer, are not available to persons detained under a preventive detention law.
Statement-II: Article 22(3) says that clauses (1) and (2) do not apply to enemy aliens and to persons arrested or detained under any law providing for preventive detention.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
questions.e: Article 22 has two parts, one for punitive and one for preventive detention. Article 22(3)(b) takes preventive detainees out of the 24-hour and lawyer safeguards, which explains Statement-I. Preventive detainees instead get protection such as the Advisory Board review.

questions.q: Under Article 23(2) of the Constitution, while imposing compulsory service for public purposes, the State shall not make any discrimination on grounds only of
o: religion, caste, place of birth or sex
questions.e: Article 23(2) permits compulsory service for public purposes, such as conscription or national service, but forbids discrimination on grounds only of religion, race, caste or class. Note that sex and place of birth appear in Article 15 but not here.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the right to freedom of religion:
1. Article 26 is available to every individual, whether or not he belongs to a religious denomination.
2. Article 27 prohibits the levy of fees by the State for the maintenance of religious institutions.
3. Article 28 prohibits religious instruction in educational institutions wholly maintained out of State funds.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Article 26 belongs to religious denominations or sections, not to individuals. Article 27 bars compulsion to pay taxes for promoting a religion; it does not bar fees. Article 28(1) bans religious instruction in wholly State-maintained institutions.

questions.q: Which one of the following writs can be issued even against a private individual?
questions.e: Habeas corpus, which orders production of a detained person, can be issued against both public authorities and private individuals illegally detaining someone. Mandamus, prohibition and certiorari generally lie against public authorities and bodies, not private persons.

questions.q:
Which of the following Directive Principles were added to Part IV by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976?
1. Equal justice and free legal aid (Article 39A)
2. Participation of workers in management of industries (Article 43A)
3. Promotion of co-operative societies (Article 43B)
4. Protection and improvement of environment, forests and wildlife (Article 48A)
How many of the above were added by that Amendment?
questions.e: The 42nd Amendment added Articles 39A, 43A and 48A, along with changes to Article 39. Article 43B on co-operative societies was added by the 97th Amendment Act, 2011.

questions.q: Which Article of the Constitution directs the State to take steps to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State?
questions.e: Article 50, a liberal-intellectual principle, aims to keep the judiciary independent of executive pressure. Article 49 concerns protection of monuments, Article 51 international peace and Article 48 agriculture and animal husbandry.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. In State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan, the Supreme Court held that Directive Principles prevail over Fundamental Rights.
2. In Minerva Mills case, the Court held that harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is an essential feature of the basic structure.
3. Directive Principles are non-justiciable but are fundamental in the governance of the country.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Champakam (1951) held the opposite: Fundamental Rights prevail, so the First Amendment was needed. Minerva Mills (1980) said the Constitution is founded on the balance between the two, and Article 37 itself says the principles are not enforceable by courts yet fundamental in governance.

questions.q:
Which of the following Directive Principles are based on Gandhian ideology?
1. Organising village panchayats
2. Promoting cottage industries on an individual or co-operative basis in rural areas
3. Prohibition of intoxicating drinks and drugs
4. Promoting the educational and economic interests of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes
5. Securing a uniform civil code
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.e: Articles 40, 43, 47 and 46 are classed as Gandhian principles, along with 43B and the ban on cow slaughter in Article 48. The uniform civil code in Article 44 is a liberal-intellectual principle.

questions.q:
Statement-I: Article 45 of the Constitution no longer directs the State to provide free and compulsory education to all children until they complete the age of fourteen years.
Statement-II: The 86th Amendment Act, 2002 inserted Article 21A as a Fundamental Right and substituted Article 45 with a provision on early childhood care and education for children below six years.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
questions.e: Once the education of children aged 6 to 14 became a Fundamental Right under Article 21A, Article 45 was recast to focus on children below six. That change is exactly why Article 45 no longer carries the earlier direction.

questions.q:
Match the following Directive Principles with the Articles:
A. Equal pay for equal work for both men and women
B. Public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness and disablement
C. Just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief
D. Equal justice and free legal aid
1. Article 39(d)
2. Article 41
3. Article 42
4. Article 39A
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.e: Equal pay for equal work is Article 39(d), public assistance is Article 41, humane conditions and maternity relief are Article 42, and free legal aid is Article 39A, added by the 42nd Amendment. Articles 41 and 42 are easily swapped.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding Fundamental Duties:
1. Part IVA containing Article 51A was inserted by the 42nd Amendment Act on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee.
2. Fundamental Duties are enforceable through writs issued by the Supreme Court.
3. Fundamental Duties apply to citizens as well as to foreigners residing in India.
4. The concept of Fundamental Duties has been borrowed from the Constitution of the erstwhile USSR.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: The Swaran Singh Committee, set up during the Emergency, recommended duties, which the 42nd Amendment inserted in 1976, and the idea comes from the Soviet Constitution. The duties are non-justiciable and addressed only to citizens, unlike many Fundamental Rights.

questions.q: Which one of the following is NOT a Fundamental Duty listed in Article 51A of the Constitution?
o: To safeguard public property and to abjure violence
To protect and improve the natural environment
To value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture
questions.e: Voting is a statutory right in India, not a duty listed in Article 51A. The other three are listed duties in Article 51A.

questions.q: The Fundamental Duty of a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to his child or ward between the age of six and fourteen years was added by the
questions.e: The original 10 duties of 1976 were joined by an 11th in 2002, when the 86th Amendment also inserted Article 21A, which made education for ages 6 to 14 a Fundamental Right. The duty on parents is the other side of that right.

questions.q:
The three new criminal laws that came into force on 1 July 2024 replaced old colonial-era laws. Consider the following statements:
1. The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 replaces the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
2. The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 replaces the Indian Evidence Act, 1872.
3. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 replaces the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita replaced the substantive Indian Penal Code, 1860, while procedure moved from the CrPC to the BNSS. Statement 3 mixes the substantive law with the procedural one.
questions.u: Justice Administration, Law Enforcement & Statutory Frameworks

questions.q:
With reference to the Supreme Court judgment in Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh (2013), consider the following statements:
1. Registration of an FIR is mandatory if the information discloses the commission of a cognizable offence.
2. A preliminary inquiry may be conducted where the information does not clearly disclose a cognizable offence.
3. Police must register an FIR even when the information discloses only a non-cognizable offence.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: The Court held that when information discloses a cognizable offence, police must register an FIR without a preliminary inquiry, but an inquiry is allowed to check whether a cognizable offence is disclosed. A non-cognizable offence goes to a daily diary entry and the informant is referred to the Magistrate.
questions.s: Lalita Kumari v. Govt. of U.P. (2013), Supreme Court
questions.u: Justice Administration, Law Enforcement & Statutory Frameworks

questions.q:
Statement-I: Reform of the police is primarily the responsibility of State Governments in India.
Statement-II: 'Police' is an entry in the State List of the Seventh Schedule.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
questions.e: Entry 2 of the State List covers police, including railway and village police, so States control recruitment, postings and administration. This is why the Supreme Court's 2006 directions in the Prakash Singh case were addressed mainly to States.
questions.s: Seventh Schedule; Prakash Singh v. Union of India (2006)
questions.u: Justice Administration, Law Enforcement & Statutory Frameworks

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding Lok Adalats:
1. The award of a Lok Adalat is deemed to be a decree of a civil court and is final and binding on the parties.
2. Lok Adalats can settle non-compoundable criminal offences.
3. The National Legal Services Authority was constituted under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, a Lok Adalat award is deemed a civil court decree and there is no appeal against it. Lok Adalats cannot deal with non-compoundable offences, since compromise is not permitted for them; NALSA gives effect to Article 39A.
questions.u: Justice Administration, Law Enforcement & Statutory Frameworks

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding amendment of the Constitution under Article 368:
1. A Bill for amendment can be introduced in either House of Parliament.
2. Prior permission of the President is required for introducing such a Bill.
3. The President is bound to give assent to a duly passed Constitution Amendment Bill.
4. A Constitution Amendment Bill can be initiated in a State Legislature.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: A Bill can start in either House and, once passed with the required majorities (and ratification when needed), the President must assent, as made clear by the 24th Amendment of 1971. No prior permission is needed and State Legislatures cannot initiate an amendment under Article 368.
questions.s: Laxmikanth, chapters on Amendment and Basic Structure

questions.q: An amendment to which one of the following requires ratification by the legislatures of at least half of the States, in addition to a special majority in Parliament?
o: Abolition of the Legislative Council of a State
questions.e: Provisions on federal structure, including the manner of election of the President, need ratification by half of the States. Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles need only a special majority, and Article 169 on Legislative Councils needs only a simple majority.
questions.s: Laxmikanth, chapters on Amendment and Basic Structure

questions.q:
Match the following cases with their holdings:
A. Shankari Prasad case
B. Golaknath case
C. Kesavananda Bharati case
D. Minerva Mills case
1. Parliament cannot amend the Fundamental Rights
2. Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution but cannot alter its basic structure
3. Parliament can amend the Fundamental Rights under Article 368
4. Limited amending power is itself a basic feature, so Parliament cannot make it absolute
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.e: Shankari Prasad (1951) upheld Parliament's power to amend Fundamental Rights, Golaknath (1967) reversed this, Kesavananda (1973) created the basic structure doctrine as a middle path, and Minerva Mills (1980) struck down clauses of the 42nd Amendment that tried to make the power absolute.
questions.s: Laxmikanth, chapters on Amendment and Basic Structure
questions.h: Shankari yes, Golaknath no, Kesavananda: basic only

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the basic structure doctrine:
1. In S. R. Bommai v. Union of India, the Supreme Court held that secularism is part of the basic structure.
2. In Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain, the Supreme Court held that Parliament's amending power is unlimited.
3. In L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India, the Supreme Court held that judicial review by the High Courts and Supreme Court is part of the basic structure.
4. Article 368 contains a list of the features that form the basic structure.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Bommai (1994) treated secularism as basic structure and Chandra Kumar (1997) held that judicial review under Articles 226 and 32 is basic. In Raj Narain (1975) the Court used the basic structure to strike down part of the 39th Amendment, so Parliament's power is not unlimited. The Constitution contains no such list; the Court has identified features case by case.
questions.s: Laxmikanth, chapters on Amendment and Basic Structure

questions.q:
Consider the following pairs:
Amendment Act : Subject
1. 52nd Amendment : Anti-defection law (Tenth Schedule)
2. 74th Amendment : Panchayati Raj institutions
3. 91st Amendment : Limiting the size of Council of Ministers
4. 101st Amendment : Reservation for economically weaker sections
How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
questions.e: The 52nd (1985) added the Tenth Schedule and the 91st (2003) capped the Council of Ministers at 15 percent of the House. The 74th Amendment is on urban local bodies (73rd is Panchayati Raj), and the 101st introduced GST; reservation for EWS came through the 103rd.
questions.s: Laxmikanth, chapters on Amendment and Basic Structure

questions.q:
Statement-I: The Indian Constitution is described as partly rigid and partly flexible.
Statement-II: Some of its provisions can be amended by a simple majority of Parliament, some by a special majority, and some require ratification by half of the States as well.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
questions.e: Articles such as 2, 3, 169 and the Fifth and Sixth Schedules can be changed by simple majority, most provisions by special majority, and federal provisions also need State ratification. This graded procedure makes the Constitution neither wholly rigid nor wholly flexible.
questions.s: Laxmikanth, chapters on Amendment and Basic Structure

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the Ninth Schedule:
1. It was added to the Constitution by the First Amendment Act, 1951.
2. In the I. R. Coelho case (2007), the Supreme Court held that laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 are open to judicial review on the ground that they violate the basic structure.
3. Laws in the Ninth Schedule are completely immune from judicial review.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: The Ninth Schedule was added to protect land reform laws from challenge. Coelho held that Ninth Schedule laws enacted after the Kesavananda judgment of 24 April 1973 can be tested against the basic structure and Fundamental Rights, so complete immunity does not exist.
questions.s: Laxmikanth, chapters on Amendment and Basic Structure

questions.q: The Constitution (99th Amendment) Act, 2014, which was struck down by the Supreme Court in October 2015, related to the
questions.e: The 99th Amendment replaced the collegium with a National Judicial Appointments Commission. In the Fourth Judges case the Supreme Court held it violated judicial independence, a basic feature, and restored the collegium system.
questions.s: Laxmikanth, chapter on Amendment of the Constitution; Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (2015)
